words.cefr_source: Unlabelled for the adjective, which is what the SAT keyed twice. Oxford labels only the verb (Oxford 5000 visible badge, C1); Cambridge shows no level.
words.def: Something that is manifest is clear and easy to see or notice. If a quality is manifest in something, that thing shows it plainly.
words.sat_sense: Adjective: plainly visible or evident. Two official keys: *manifest in* (= evident from) and *manifest* in a literary 'most nearly means' item (= perceptible).
ex: The architect's debt to traditional Japanese design is manifest in the sliding screens and open courtyards of her early houses.
Fah's love of maps was manifest in every page of her geography project, down to the hand-drawn compass in each corner.
words.grammar: Adjective: *be / become manifest (in something)*. Verb: *manifest something* or reflexive *manifest itself in / as something* (*the illness manifests itself as a rash*). Formal in every use.
words.say: /ˈmænɪfest/: three syllables, stress on MAN for the adjective, verb and noun alike; the last syllable is a clear *fest*.
words.fact: From Latin *manifestus*, 'plain, caught in the act'. One possible story is that it joins *manus* ('hand') to a second part meaning 'struck' or 'seized', so that a manifest thief was one caught by hand; the second part is uncertain. A ship's *manifest* is the list that makes its cargo plain.
words.trap: The self-help sense ('manifest your dreams') is not the academic one. *Manifest* is about being visible, not about being important or being true.
distractor_traps: As key *manifest in* it beat *insensible to*, *scrutinized by* and *complicated by*: only *manifest in* says the quality shows itself there. The preposition does half the work.
In the 'most nearly means' item the answer was 'perceptible', against 'realized', 'situated' and 'dwindling': the wrong options borrow the verb sense (make real) or simply fit the scene.
words.tip: A ship's manifest puts the cargo on show: what is manifest is on show.

mini_item.passage: The composer never wrote about her childhood on the coast. Its influence is nonetheless ______ her late symphonies, where slow, swelling phrases rise and fall like waves and a solitary horn suggests a distant ship.
mini_item.rationale: *Nonetheless* signals that the influence can be clearly seen despite her silence, and the wave-like music is the visible sign; the other options deny or reverse that.

words.cefr_source: Unlabelled: no level on the Oxford or Cambridge entry for *ambivalent* or *ambivalence* (entry pages read 25 Nov 2026). Treat as beyond C1.
words.def: If you are ambivalent about something, you have two opposite feelings about it at the same time, so you cannot simply say you are for it or against it.
words.sat_sense: Mixed feelings that pull in two directions. The official key is the noun phrase *ambivalence toward*; the adjective appears more often as a tempting wrong option.
ex: Early reviewers were ambivalent about the novel, praising its inventive structure while complaining that its characters felt cold.
Praew is ambivalent about moving to the science stream: she loves biology, but she would miss her literature class.
words.grammar: Adjective after *be / feel / remain* + *about* or *towards*. Noun *ambivalence* + *about / toward(s)*. The subject is a person or group, or their attitude, response or reaction: *critics were ambivalent*, *an ambivalent reaction*; not *the data were ambivalent*.
words.say: /æmˈbɪvələnt/: four syllables, stress on BIV: am-BIV-uh-luhnt. Do not stress the first syllable.
words.ukus: British English prefers *towards*; American English, and the SAT, write *toward*. Both are correct.
words.fact: The word is only about a century old. The Swiss psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler coined German *Ambivalenz* in 1910 from Latin *ambi-* ('on both sides') and *valentia* ('strength'), on the model of *equivalence*: two feelings of equal strength pulling opposite ways.
words.trap: Not *indifferent* (no feeling at all), and not *ambiguous* (two possible meanings: used for words and evidence, not for people's feelings).
distractor_traps: As the key (*ambivalence toward*) it beat *responsiveness to*, *renunciation of* and *mastery over*: only ambivalence names two opposed attitudes at once. Check that the passage gives BOTH a positive and a negative reaction.

As a wrong option it sat beside the keys *counterfactual* (with *retrospective*, *analogical*) and *opaque* (with *abrasive*, *outspoken*): if the blank describes an analysis or a piece of writing rather than someone's feelings, *ambivalent* cannot fit.
words.tip: *Ambi-* = both (as in *ambidextrous*, both hands) + *valent* = strong: both feelings are strong.

words.cefr_source: Oxford visible badge (Oxford 5000, C1); Cambridge badge also C1.
words.def: If something is integral to a thing, it is an essential part of it, and the thing would not be complete or would not work without it.
words.sat_sense: Essential, built into the whole: the 'centre' end of the centre-to-edge scale.
ex: Far from being decoration, the chorus is integral to Greek tragedy, since it tells the audience how to judge the action.
Mint's careful timekeeping was integral to the debate team's win; without her signals, every speaker would have run over.
words.grammar: *integral to + noun* or *an integral part / element / component of + noun*. Not *integral for*; *in* appears only in the frame *an integral role / part in + noun or -ing*.
words.say: /ˈɪntɪɡrəl/: stress on IN: IN-ti-gruhl. (Some speakers say in-TEG-ral, especially in maths; IN-ti-gruhl is the safe choice.)
words.fact: From Latin *integer*, 'whole, untouched': *in-* ('not') plus the root of *tangere* ('to touch'). An integer is a whole number, integrity is being whole in character, and an integral part is one the whole cannot lose.
words.trap: Stronger than *important* or *useful*. A helpful extra is not integral. In maths *an integral* is a noun (calculus); the SAT uses the adjective.
distractor_traps: Official wrong options beside it: *tangential*, *subsequent*, *analogous* (Practice Test 11). *Tangential* is its opposite on the centre-to-edge scale and comes from the same Latin root, *tangere*: it only touches the edge.
In a second official item: *antithetical*, *resigned*, *invulnerable*. *Antithetical to* means directly opposed to; the passage will show whether the part belongs to the whole or fights it.
words.tip: An *integer* is a whole number; an *integral* part keeps the whole whole.

words.cefr_source: Oxford page markup (C1 on the idiom *that said / having said that*; not a displayed badge). Cambridge shows no level.
words.def: You use *that said* to add something that limits, or partly goes against, what you have just said, without taking the first statement back.
words.sat_sense: Concession: both statements stay true, and the second one qualifies the first. Tested in Transitions questions, not Words in Context.
ex: The survey reached more than ten thousand households. That said, almost all of them were in cities, so its findings may not hold for rural areas.
Ploy's presentation ran two minutes over the limit. That said, it was the only one the whole class remembered a week later.
words.grammar: Starts a new sentence (or follows a semicolon) and takes a comma: *X. That said, Y.* It links two full statements; it cannot join a clause to a phrase.
words.say: /ˌðæt ˈsed/: the main stress falls on *said*; pause briefly after it.
words.ukus: *Having said that* is the commoner form in British speech; *that said* and *that being said* are normal in both varieties and in SAT options.
words.fact: It is a shortened absolute clause: *that (having been) said*. The grammar itself tells you the logic: the first point has been said and stands, and now comes the limit.
words.trap: *That is* restates; *that said* concedes. Recall from the Dec 2024 sitting reported students confusing exactly this pair.
distractor_traps: In the official items where it is the key it sits beside result words (*thus*, *for this reason*), addition words (*moreover*) and example or restatement words (*for example*, *in other words*, *specifically*). Test: does sentence 2 follow from sentence 1 (result), add to it (addition), illustrate or restate it, or pull against it without cancelling it (*that said*)?
It is a wrong option in eight official items, mostly Hard: when sentence 2 simply continues or explains sentence 1, *that said* is the trap.
words.tip: Read it as 'I have said that, and I still mean it, BUT...'.

words.cefr_source: Unlabelled: no level on the Oxford or Cambridge entry for either sense (entry pages read 25 Nov 2026). Treat as beyond C1.
words.def: Opaque writing, rules or reasons are difficult to understand because they are not made clear. Literally, an opaque material does not let light through.
words.sat_sense: The figurative sense: unclear, hard to understand. Used of prose, methods, motives, decisions and systems.
ex: The committee's reasons for rejecting the paper remained opaque, since its report gave no account of how the reviewers had reached their decision.
The scoring rules for the science fair were so opaque that Mint had to ask three different teachers what 'originality' meant.
words.grammar: Before a noun or after *be / remain / seem*; *opaque to + person* (*opaque to most readers*). Gradable: *fairly / increasingly opaque*.
words.say: /əʊˈpeɪk/: two syllables, stress on the second: oh-PAYK. The *-que* is just /k/. The noun *opacity* is /əʊˈpæsəti/ (oh-PASS-uh-tee).
words.fact: From Latin *opacus*, 'shaded, dark'; where *opacus* itself came from is unknown. In English it first meant 'shaded, dark', then 'not letting light through' (from the 1640s), and from 1761 'hard to understand'.
words.trap: Opaque does not mean false, secret or complicated: it means you cannot see how it works. A simple rule can be opaque if nobody explains it.
distractor_traps: Official options in one Hard item: *authoritative*, *empirical*, *facile*. These praise or classify the writing; *opaque* is the only one about clarity. (*Facile* = too easy, shallow.)
In a second Hard item: *abrasive*, *ambivalent*, *outspoken*. All three describe a person's manner; *opaque* describes how hard the text or process is to see into.
words.tip: Opaque glass: light cannot get through. Opaque prose: meaning cannot get through.

words.cefr_source: Unlabelled: no level on the Oxford or Cambridge entry. Treat as beyond C1.
words.def: A tenuous link, claim or position is so weak or slight that it could easily be broken or shown to be wrong.
words.sat_sense: Weak, thinly supported: the bottom rung of the strength-of-claim ladder. Typical subjects are *link, connection, claim, evidence, grasp, hold*.
ex: Critics argue that the link between the two manuscripts is tenuous, resting on a single shared spelling error.
Fern's claim that she had lost her homework on the train was tenuous at best, as she had cycled to school that day.
words.grammar: Before a noun (*a tenuous link*) or after *be / seem / remain*. Often followed by *at best*. It describes links, claims and positions, not people.
words.say: /ˈtenjuəs/: three syllables, TEN-yoo-uhs. Do not say ten-OO-us.
words.fact: From Latin *tenuis*, 'thin', a distant relative of English *thin* itself. A tenuous argument is a thread stretched thin. The same root gives *attenuate* (make thinner or weaker) and *extenuating* circumstances (ones that thin out the blame).
words.trap: Not *tentative* (offered cautiously, may change) and not *untenable* (cannot be defended at all). Tenuous = still standing, but only just.
distractor_traps: Practice Test 5 options: *enduring*, *contentious*, *conspicuous*. *Enduring* is the opposite direction (lasting); *contentious* means argued about, which a strong claim can also be; *conspicuous* is about visibility.
Harder-module item options: *disorienting*, *nuanced*, *unoriginal*. All are criticisms, but only *tenuous* attacks how well the claim is supported.
words.tip: A *ten*uous link is a *thin* one: the two words are distant cousins.

words.cefr_source: Unlabelled: no level on the Oxford or Cambridge entry for *anomaly* or *anomalous*. Treat as beyond C1.
words.def: An anomaly is something that is different from what is normal or expected, so that it does not fit the pattern around it.
words.sat_sense: A result, case or feature that breaks an otherwise regular pattern: the standard research word for 'the odd one out'.
ex: The single warm year in the tree-ring record was at first dismissed as an anomaly, but later samples showed the same spike.
Mali's 42 in maths was an anomaly: she had scored above 85 in every other test this term.
words.grammar: Countable: *an anomaly*, *anomalies in the data*. Adjective *anomalous* goes before a noun (*an anomalous result*) or after *be*.
words.say: Noun /əˈnɒməli/: uh-NOM-uh-lee. Adjective /əˈnɒmələs/: uh-NOM-uh-luhs. Stress on NOM in both.
words.fact: From Greek *anomalos*, 'uneven': *an-* ('not') + *homalos* ('even'), which comes from *homos* ('same'). So *anomaly* and *homogeneous* share a root. It is not built on *nomos* ('law'), although 'breaks the law of the pattern' is a handy way to remember it.
words.trap: An anomaly is not an error and not a mystery: it is a mismatch with a pattern. No pattern in the passage, no anomaly.
distractor_traps: As key it beat *hypothesis*, *affinity* and *corroboration*: all research nouns, but only *anomaly* names a result that does not fit. *Corroboration* is the opposite idea (a result that supports).
Recall reports name *anomaly / anomalies / anomalous* as wrong options on three 2026 dates: it is wrong when the passage's case is simply new or rare but fits the pattern.
words.tip: An *anomaly* is a-normal: it sits outside the normal pattern.

mini_item.passage: Of the forty tide gauges along the coast, thirty-nine recorded a steady rise in sea level over the decade. The fortieth showed a slight fall, ______ that the team traced to the slow uplift of the land beneath that one station.

words.cefr_source: Unlabelled for the adjective. Oxford marks only the computing noun (C2, page markup); Cambridge shows no level.
words.def: Something peripheral is at the edge of a thing, or is not as important as its main part.
words.sat_sense: Figurative: of minor importance to the main subject (*peripheral to the debate*). The 'edge' end of the centre-to-edge scale.
ex: For decades, women's letters were treated as peripheral to the study of the period, useful for colour but not for evidence.
Aom's group spent so long on peripheral details, like the font of the poster, that they never rehearsed the talk itself.
words.grammar: *peripheral to + noun*; before a noun: *a peripheral figure / role / issue*. Noun: *on the periphery of something*.
words.say: /pəˈrɪfərəl/: four syllables, stress on RIF: puh-RIF-uh-ruhl. The *ph* is /f/.
words.fact: From Greek *peripheria*, 'circumference': *peri* ('around') + *pherein* ('to carry'), so literally the line carried round the outside. *Peri-* also gives *perimeter* and *periscope*.
words.trap: Peripheral is about position and importance, not visibility. A peripheral figure can be easy to see; a central one can be hidden.
distractor_traps: Practice Test 10 options: *unobtrusive*, *concealed*, *approximate*. *Unobtrusive* (not attracting attention) and *concealed* (hidden) belong to the hidden/visible field; the passage was about how central something was, not how noticeable.
Its true opposites, *integral* and *central*, are the words to test it against: is the thing part of the core or at the edge?
words.tip: *Peri-* = around, as in *perimeter*: peripheral things sit on the perimeter.

words.cefr_source: Oxford page markup (C2 in a hidden attribute; no badge is displayed). Cambridge shows no level.
words.def: If you are sanguine about something, you are cheerful and confident that it will turn out well, often when other people are worried.
words.sat_sense: Optimistic, especially in a difficult situation (College Board's own gloss is 'optimistic'). Nothing to do with blood in modern use.
ex: While most economists predicted a long recession, a few remained sanguine about the prospects for recovery.
Bua is surprisingly sanguine about the netball final, even though two of her team's best players are injured.
words.grammar: After *be / remain / seem* + *about + noun*, or before *view / outlook / prediction*. Very often negative or comparative: *less sanguine*, *not so sanguine*.
words.say: /ˈsæŋɡwɪn/: two syllables, SANG-gwin. The ending rhymes with *win*, not *wine*.
words.fact: From Latin *sanguis*, 'blood'. Medieval medicine taught that the body held four fluids, or humours, and that a person ruled by blood was red-cheeked, lively and hopeful. The medicine was abandoned; the adjective for the hopeful temperament stayed.
words.trap: *Sanguinary* means bloodthirsty: a completely different word. And sanguine is quiet confidence, not enthusiasm or happiness.
distractor_traps: Practice Test 10 options: *recalcitrant* (stubbornly refusing to obey), *misanthropic* (disliking people), *earnest* (serious and sincere). All four are rare temperament words; only *sanguine* is about expecting a good outcome.
This is the model 'attitude' item: find the outlook the passage describes (hopeful, resistant, hostile, serious) before looking at the options.
words.tip: Blood in the cheeks, a healthy glow, a hopeful face: sanguine.

words.cefr_source: Oxford page markup (C2 in a hidden attribute; no badge is displayed). Cambridge shows no level.
words.def: To ameliorate a bad situation or a problem is to make it better, though not necessarily to solve it completely.
words.sat_sense: Improve something bad: the 'remedy' end of the remedy-to-worsen scale. The object is a problem, a condition or its effects.
ex: Planting mangroves along the estuary was intended to ameliorate the effects of coastal erosion on nearby villages.
The new covered walkway has ameliorated the morning crush at the school gate, though the queue is still long.
words.grammar: Transitive: *ameliorate + a problem / conditions / the effects of something*. The object is the bad thing, never a person: not *ameliorate the patients*.
words.say: /əˈmiːliəreɪt/: five syllables, stress on MEE: uh-MEE-lee-uh-rayt.
words.fact: From French *améliorer*, built on Latin *melior*, 'better'. English first had *meliorate*; the *a-* was added later under French influence. Spanish *mejor* and Italian *migliore* ('better') are cousins.
words.trap: Only bad things are ameliorated. You *improve* a good essay; you *ameliorate* poor conditions. It does not mean 'solve'.
distractor_traps: Practice Test 5 options: *sanction*, *rationalize*, *postulate*. Each is a formal verb that a reader half-knows; none means 'make better'. *Sanction* is a classic trap because it can mean approve or punish.
In the sister item keyed *redressing*, the wrong options included *exacerbating*: same field, opposite direction. Decide first whether the passage wants the problem better or worse.
words.tip: a·[melior]·ate: *melior* = better (think Spanish *mejor*). Make it better.

words.cefr_source: Unlabelled: no level on the Oxford or Cambridge entry for *immaterial*. Treat as beyond C1.
words.def: If something is immaterial to a question or decision, it is not important or relevant to it and makes no difference.
words.sat_sense: Irrelevant, making no difference to the matter in hand. Not the older sense 'without physical form'.
ex: The age of the manuscript is immaterial to the argument, which concerns only the meaning of its final line.
Whether Fah presents first or last is immaterial to her mark, because every group is judged on the same rubric.
words.grammar: *immaterial to + noun*; or *It is immaterial whether / who / how + clause*. Not *immaterial for*.
words.say: /ˌɪməˈtɪəriəl/: five syllables, stress on TEER: im-uh-TEER-ee-uhl.
words.fact: From medieval Latin *immaterialis*, 'not made of matter'. The 'unimportant' sense dates from the 1690s and comes from *material* in its sixteenth-century sense 'important' (still used in law, where *material evidence* is evidence that matters to the case). So *immaterial* means, almost literally, 'it does not matter'.
words.trap: *Material* as an adjective means important or relevant (*a material fact*), so *immaterial* is its opposite, not a word about cloth or physical stuff.
distractor_traps: Recall reports do not give the other options. In its official sister item, the key *inconsequential to* beat *controversial among*, *antagonistic toward* and *imitated by*: the trap is another adjective + preposition that fits the grammar but states a different relationship.
The contrast to master is with *integral to* (cannot do without it), *contingent on* (depends on it) and *peripheral to* (at the edge of it): four relevance relationships, four prepositions to check.
words.tip: Im-material: it doesn't *matter*.

words.cefr_source: Unlabelled: no level on the Oxford or Cambridge entry (entry pages read 25 Nov 2026). Treat as beyond C1.
words.def: A homogeneous group or substance is made up of people or parts that are all of the same kind.
words.sat_sense: All alike throughout: the 'sameness' pole opposite *disparate*, *diverse* and *heterogeneous*. Used of populations, samples, mixtures and styles.
ex: Because the sample was homogeneous, drawn entirely from one university's first-year students, the findings may not apply to older adults.
The playlist for the class party was oddly homogeneous: forty T-pop songs in a row and nothing else.
words.grammar: Before a noun or after *be*; often with an adverb of respect: *ethnically / culturally / genetically homogeneous*.
words.say: /ˌhɒməˈdʒiːniəs/: five syllables, main stress on JEE: hom-uh-JEE-nee-uhs. The noun *homogeneity* is /ˌhɒmədʒəˈniːəti/.
words.ukus: The four-syllable spelling *homogenous* (huh-MOJ-uh-nuhs) is common in American use; British dictionaries and the SAT's printed options use *homogeneous*.
words.fact: From Greek *homos* ('same') + *genos* ('kind'). Its twin *heterogeneous* swaps in *heteros* ('other'). Homogenised milk has been processed so that the cream is the same all the way through.
words.trap: It describes the make-up of a group, not agreement between people (*unanimous*) and not equality (*equal*). A homogeneous class can still disagree.
distractor_traps: Official Medium item options: *uncontroversial*, *individualistic*, *theoretical*. *Individualistic* is the opposite direction (each one different).

Official Hard item options: *depleted*, *immature*, *dispersed*. All describe a population; only *homogeneous* is about how alike its members are. *Dispersed* is about where they are, not what they are like.
words.tip: *Homo-* = same, *gen-* = kind (as in *genre*, *gene*): the same kind all through.

words.cefr_source: Unlabelled for the adjective. Oxford marks only the military-group sense of the noun (C2, page markup); Cambridge shows no level.
words.def: If one thing is contingent on another, it will happen or be true only if the other thing happens or is true.
words.sat_sense: Conditional dependence: A occurs only if B does. Formal sister of *dependent on*.
ex: The spread of the plant is contingent on the presence of a single species of moth that pollinates it.
Khao's place on the field trip is contingent on her handing in the consent form by Friday.
words.grammar: *be contingent on / upon + noun or -ing*: *contingent on receiving approval*. Only *on* or *upon*; not *contingent to* or *contingent with*.
words.say: /kənˈtɪndʒənt/: three syllables, stress on TIN: kuhn-TIN-juhnt.
words.fact: From Latin *contingere*, 'to touch, to happen': *con-* ('together') + *tangere* ('to touch'). An event contingent on another 'touches' it and cannot occur alone. The same root hides in *integral*, *tangent*, *tangible* and *contact*.
words.trap: As a noun, *a contingent* is a group (*the Thai contingent at the conference*). And *contingent* does not mean 'likely' or 'continuing'.
distractor_traps: As key it beat *inhibited by*, *obligated to* and *reserved for*: three more adjective + preposition frames. *Inhibited by* is a blocking relationship; only *contingent on* says 'happens only if'.
As a wrong option beside the key *saturated with* (with *susceptible to*, *depleted of*): there the passage described how much of something was present, not a condition.
words.tip: con·[ting]·ent: the two events are touching (*tangere*); pull one away and the other falls.

words.cefr_source: Unlabelled: no level on the Oxford or Cambridge entry for *attest* (entry pages read 25 Nov 2026). Treat as beyond C1.
words.def: If one thing attests to another, it shows or proves that the other thing exists or is true. If a person attests to something, they state that it is true.
words.sat_sense: With a thing as subject: 'serve as evidence of'. In academic prose the evidence, not a person, usually does the attesting.
ex: Thousands of shell beads found far inland attest to the reach of the coastal traders' networks.
The worn steps of the old school library attest to the generations of girls who have climbed them.
words.grammar: *attest to + noun / the fact that* is the usual pattern in SAT-style prose. Also *attest that + clause*, and a formal or legal transitive use, *attest something* (*attest a will*). The subject is usually plural evidence (*records, finds, letters attest to*), so check agreement: *attest*, not *attests*.
words.say: /əˈtest/: two syllables, stress on TEST: uh-TEST. In the phrase, *to* is weak: /tə/ before a consonant, /tu/ before a vowel.
words.fact: From Latin *attestari*: *ad-* ('to') + *testari* ('to bear witness'), from *testis*, 'a witness'. The same witness stands behind *testify*, *testimony*, *testament*, *contest* and *protest*.
words.trap: Before a noun, expect *attest to* (*the finds attest to its age*); the bare transitive *attest something* exists but is formal or legal. Do not confuse with *attribute to* (say what caused something).
distractor_traps: No official Words in Context item with this key was found. Recall of the Aug 2025 sitting lists it beside *collude with*: both are verb + preposition, so the test is which relationship the passage shows (giving evidence of, or secretly cooperating with).
Official grammar evidence: Practice Test 8 (Module 1, Q23) uses *attest* as the verb in a subject-verb agreement item, where the trap was the singular *attests* after a long plural subject.
words.tip: *Test-* = witness, as in *testify*: the evidence takes the witness stand.

words.cefr_source: Unlabelled: no level on the Oxford or Cambridge entry for *incongruous*. Treat as beyond C1.
words.def: If something is incongruous with its surroundings or with what you know, it seems strange because it does not match or fit them.
words.sat_sense: Not fitting, out of keeping with: a mismatch between a thing and its setting, or between a finding and a theory.
ex: The cheerful tone of the final chapter is incongruous with the bleak events that it describes.
A glass coffee bar would look incongruous with the old wooden shophouses along the canal near Ploy's home.
words.grammar: *incongruous with + noun*. Alone before a noun or after *look / seem*: *an incongruous detail*; *it looked incongruous in the old street*.
words.say: /ɪnˈkɒŋɡruəs/: four syllables, stress on KONG: in-KONG-groo-uhs.
words.fact: From Latin *in-* ('not') + *congruus* ('agreeing, suitable'), from *congruere*, 'to come together, to agree'. Geometry kept the positive form: congruent triangles fit each other exactly.
words.trap: Not *inconsistent* (two statements that cannot both be true) and not *incompatible* (two things that cannot work together). Incongruous = looks or feels out of place.
distractor_traps: *Incongruous* is an official wrong option beside the key *unassuming* (with *shrewd*, *pretentious*) in Practice Test 11: the passage described something plain and modest, with no mismatch in sight.
Recall of the Nov 2025 sitting names *inconsistencies* and *incompatibilities* together as options: learn the three *in-con-* words as a set and ask which kind of misfit the passage shows.
words.tip: *Congruent* triangles fit exactly; *in-congruous* things do not fit.

words.cefr_source: Unlabelled: no level on the Oxford or Cambridge entry for any sense of *proxy* (entry pages read 25 Nov 2026). Treat as beyond C1.
words.def: A proxy for something is a thing you measure or use in its place, because the real thing cannot be measured or observed directly.
words.sat_sense: The research sense: a stand-in measure (*tree rings are proxies for past rainfall*), not the legal sense (a person who acts for you) or the computing sense (a proxy server).
ex: Because ancient temperatures cannot be measured directly, researchers use the width of tree rings as a proxy for past climate.
In her survey of M4 students, Nam used the number of library visits as a proxy for how much each student read.
colls: use X as a proxy for Y
words.grammar: Countable noun + *for*: *X is / serves as a proxy for Y*; plural *proxies for*. The pattern is always the measurable thing first, the unmeasurable thing after *for*.
words.say: /ˈprɒksi/: PROK-see, two syllables, stress on the first. Plural /ˈprɒksiz/.
words.fact: *Proxy* is a squeezed form of *procuracy*, from Latin *procurare*, 'to manage on someone's behalf'. It first meant a person acting for another (as in acting *by proxy*); science later borrowed it for one measurement acting for another.
words.trap: A proxy is not a cause, a sign of the future or an example. It stands in for something it is believed to track.
distractor_traps: Official Hard item options: *contrivances of*, *catalysts of*, *deterrents to*. A *catalyst of* X causes X and a *deterrent to* X discourages X: both are cause words. A *proxy for* X only measures X.

TTA's vendor list (unverified) also names *harbingers of* and *emissaries for* as distractors: a *harbinger of* X announces that X is coming. Ask: is the thing causing, announcing or standing in for X?
words.tip: A proxy stands in for someone who cannot be there; a proxy measure stands in for something you cannot measure.

words.cefr_source: Oxford visible badge on the headword *prevail* (Oxford 5000, C1), though Oxford's 'defeat an opponent' sense itself carries no label; Cambridge gives C2 for its 'get control or influence' sense.
words.def: If one person, idea or force prevails over another, it proves stronger and wins in the end, usually after a struggle.
words.sat_sense: Win out over a competitor: used of theories, interests, species, designs and arguments as well as people.
ex: In the long dispute over the fossil's age, the geologists' estimate eventually prevailed over the one based on anatomy.
Pim's calm, evidence-based case prevailed over the louder arguments of the other team in the semi-final.
words.grammar: Intransitive + *over* (or *against*) + the loser: *A prevailed over B*. Different verb patterns: *prevail in / among* = be common; *prevail on / upon someone to do something* = persuade.
words.say: /prɪˈveɪl/: two syllables, stress on VAIL: pri-VAYL.
words.fact: From Latin *praevalere*: *prae* ('before, ahead') + *valere* ('to be strong'). To prevail is to be stronger and so come out ahead. *Valere* also gives *valid*, *value*, *valiant* and the *-valent* of *ambivalent*.
words.trap: *Prevail* alone often means 'be widespread' (*the view that prevailed at the time*); *prevalent* means common, not victorious. The preposition tells you which sense you have.
distractor_traps: *Prevail* is an official wrong option in a Hard item keyed *intersect*, beside *succumb* and *diverge*: *prevail* and *succumb* are opposites (win, give way), and neither fitted two things that simply cross.
Check direction: in *A prevails over B* the winner comes first. A passage in which the first-named side loses needs *succumb to* or *yield to*.
words.tip: pre·[vail]: *valere* = be strong, like *value* and *valid*. The stronger one prevails.

words.cefr_source: Unlabelled: no level on the Oxford or Cambridge entry for *inconsequential*. Treat as beyond C1.
words.def: If something is inconsequential to a person or a matter, it is not important to them and has no real effect.
words.sat_sense: Unimportant because it has no consequences for the matter in hand.
ex: The exact date of the letter is inconsequential to the historian's case, which depends only on who received it.
A two-baht rise in the price of iced tea is inconsequential to most students, but the canteen sells a thousand cups a day.
words.grammar: *inconsequential to + noun*; alone before a noun: *an inconsequential error*. Often after *seemingly / apparently*, when the writer is about to show that the thing mattered after all.
words.say: /ɪnˌkɒnsɪˈkwenʃl/: five syllables, main stress on KWEN: in-kon-si-KWEN-shuhl.
words.fact: Built from *in-* ('not') + *consequential*, from Latin *consequi*, 'to follow closely'. Something inconsequential is something nothing follows from. *Sequel*, *sequence* and *consecutive* come from the same 'follow' root.
words.trap: It judges effects, not size: a small change can be consequential, and a huge effort can be inconsequential. *Inconsistent* is a different word.
distractor_traps: Practice Test 6 options: *controversial among*, *antagonistic toward*, *imitated by*. Each is adjective + preposition, so grammar will not help; decide what relationship the passage states (did not matter to, was argued over by, was hostile to, was copied by).
Neighbours that could sit beside it: *immaterial to* (irrelevant to a question) and *negligible* (a size word: too small to count, with no *to*).
words.tip: No *consequence* follows: in-consequential.

words.cefr_source: Unlabelled: no level on the Oxford or Cambridge entry. Treat as beyond C1.
words.def: To substantiate a claim is to provide evidence or facts that show it is true.
words.sat_sense: Support a claim with evidence. It differs from *corroborate* in that you can substantiate your own claim, whereas corroboration comes from a second, independent source.
ex: The journalist could not substantiate her claim that the painting was a forgery, since the laboratory report had never been published.
Mook substantiated her complaint about the canteen queue with a week of timings recorded on her phone.
words.grammar: Transitive: *substantiate + a claim / allegation / theory*. The negative adjective *unsubstantiated* is at least as common as the verb.
words.say: /səbˈstænʃieɪt/: four syllables, stress on STAN: suhb-STAN-shee-ayt.
words.fact: From Latin *substantia*, 'substance', literally 'that which stands under' (*sub-* + *stare*, 'to stand'). To substantiate a claim is to put something solid underneath it.
words.trap: *Substantial* means large; *substantiate* means support with evidence. A claim can be substantial and unsubstantiated.
distractor_traps: It is an official wrong option in two Medium items: beside the key *negating* (with *prefiguring*, *entrenching*) and beside the key *marginalize* (with *epitomize*, *extol*). In both, the passage wanted a verb that weakens or pushes aside, and *substantiate* runs the opposite way.
Its near-twins on the same side are *corroborate*, *validate* and *buttress*: when two of them appear together, check who supplies the support (the claimant, or an independent source).
words.tip: Give the claim some *substance*: substantiate it.

words.cefr_source: Unlabelled: no level on the Oxford or Cambridge entry for *dearth* (or for its synonym *paucity*). Treat as beyond C1.
words.def: A dearth of something is a lack of it: there is not enough, or there are not enough.
words.sat_sense: Scarcity, in the frame *a dearth of + noun*. Its official twin is *a paucity of*, a Hard Question Bank key.
ex: Research on the language has been held back by a dearth of written records from before 1800.
There is a dearth of shade on the school field, so the M3 football club now trains at seven in the morning.
words.grammar: Singular with *a* (or *the*) + *of* + plural or uncountable noun: *a dearth of studies / evidence*. The verb agrees with *dearth*: *a dearth of records has hampered...*
words.say: /dɜːθ/: one syllable, rhymes with *earth* and *birth*; it does not sound like *death* or *dear*.
words.fact: *Dearth* is *dear* + *-th*, built like *warmth* and *width*. It first meant dearness, a time when food was costly because there was too little of it, and from there simply scarcity.
words.trap: Sounds like *death* but has nothing to do with it. Opposite direction from *a wealth of*, *an abundance of* and *a profusion of*.
distractor_traps: In the official item keyed *paucity of*, the options were *quarrel about*, *profusion of* and *verisimilitude in*: *profusion of* is the same frame with the opposite meaning (a great quantity).
Quantity frames to keep apart: *a dearth / paucity of* (too little), *a profusion / wealth of* (a great deal), *a preponderance of* (the larger share).
words.tip: When rice is *dear* (expensive), there is a *dearth* of it.

words.cefr_source: Oxford visible badge (Oxford 5000, C1), with C1 on both senses. Cambridge shows no level.
words.def: You use *accordingly* to say that something happens as a result of what has just been mentioned, and in a way that suits it.
words.sat_sense: Result with a sense of fit: because of X, someone did Y, which was the appropriate response. Tested in Transitions questions.
ex: The first trial showed that the dose was too low to have any effect. Accordingly, the researchers doubled it in the second.
The forecast warned of heavy rain all afternoon. Accordingly, Ploy's class moved its plant survey from the park to the greenhouse.
words.grammar: As a transition it opens the sentence and takes a comma: *Accordingly, the team...* At the end of a clause it is an adverb of manner: *read the rules and act accordingly* (= in the way that fits).
words.say: /əˈkɔːdɪŋli/: four syllables, stress on CORD: uh-KOR-ding-lee.
words.fact: *Accord* comes through French from Latin *ad-* ('to') + *cor* ('heart'): to bring hearts together, hence to agree. Something done *accordingly* agrees with what went before. (The *cor-* of *corroborate* is a different thing: it is the prefix *com-*.)
words.trap: Not *according to* (which names a source). And it cannot introduce a contrast, an example or a restatement.
distractor_traps: In its three official items the wrong options include *In contrast*, *In other words* and *In the end*: check that sentence 2 is a response caused by sentence 1, not a restatement of it and not merely the last step in time.
It is itself a wrong option in two official items. If sentence 2 is a fact that would be true anyway, no result word fits.
words.tip: In *accord* with what came before: the action matches the reason.

words.def: To corroborate a statement, theory or finding is to provide new evidence, from a separate source, that supports it.
words.sat_sense: Confirm by adding independent evidence. Near the top of the strength-of-claim ladder: a corroborated finding has been supported twice.
ex: Excavations at the harbour corroborated the chronicle's account of a great fire, revealing a thick layer of ash from the same decade.
Mint said the projector had been broken all week, and the technician's repair log corroborated her story.
words.grammar: Transitive; the subject is the new evidence or the second witness: *the log corroborated her story*. Very common in the passive: *was corroborated by later studies*.
words.say: /kəˈrɒbəreɪt/: four syllables, stress on ROB: kuh-ROB-uh-rayt. Do not turn it into *collaborate*.
words.fact: From Latin *corroborare*, 'to strengthen': *com-* (here simply 'thoroughly', and nothing to do with *cor*, 'heart') + *robur*, 'oak, strength'. *Robust* is from the same oak. To corroborate a claim is to make it oak-strong.
words.trap: *Collaborate* = work together. *Corroborate* = back up with evidence. You cannot corroborate your own claim by repeating it.
distractor_traps: Practice Test 7 options: *circumvent* (find a way round), *disseminate* (spread widely), *implement* (put into effect). All are things a researcher might do with a rule, a result or a plan; only *corroborate* is what new evidence does to a claim.
The noun *corroboration* is itself an official wrong option beside the key *anomaly*: a result that fits and supports is the opposite of one that stands out.
words.tip: cor·[rob]·orate: *robur* = oak, as in *robust*. Evidence that makes the claim robust.

words.def: Disparate things are so different from each other in kind that they are difficult to compare or to bring together.
words.sat_sense: Fundamentally unlike. Typically of sources, groups, fields or elements that someone brings together: the 'difference' pole opposite *homogeneous*.

words.grammar: Almost always before a plural noun (*disparate fields*) or after *as* in *as disparate as X and Y*. It compares members of a set, so it needs two or more things.
words.say: /ˈdɪspərət/: three syllables, stress on DIS, and the last syllable is a weak /ət/: DIS-puh-ruht. Not dis-PAIR-ayt.
words.fact: From Latin *disparatus*, 'separated', from *disparare*: *dis-* ('apart') + *parare* ('to prepare, set'). Its meaning was coloured by Latin *dispar*, 'unequal', which is where *disparity* comes from.
words.trap: It is not *desperate* (/ˈdespərət/, in great need), which sounds almost the same. And a *disparity* is a gap, often an unfair one, not merely a difference in kind.
distractor_traps: Official options: *complementary*, *unknown*, *interchangeable*. *Complementary* things differ but complete each other; *interchangeable* things are so alike you can swap them. The passage decides whether the differences fit together, cancel out or simply stand.

words.def: Something latent exists but is hidden and is not yet active, developed or noticeable.
words.sat_sense: Present but not yet showing (College Board's gloss is 'dormant'). The 'hidden' pole opposite *manifest*.

words.def: If one thing belies another, it gives a false idea of it, or it shows that it cannot be true.
words.sat_sense: Two linked uses: (1) a surface belies the reality beneath it (*her calm voice belied her nerves*); (2) facts belie a claim (*the figures belie the report's optimism*). In both, appearance and truth point in different directions.
ex: The plain cover of the notebook belies the importance of its contents, which include the first sketch of the engine.
Mook's relaxed smile belied how nervous she felt before her English speech at morning assembly.
words.grammar: Transitive, no preposition: *X belies Y*. Forms: *belies, belied, belying*. In use (1) the subject is the appearance and the object is the truth; in use (2) the subject is the evidence and the object is the false claim.
words.say: /bɪˈlaɪ/: two syllables, stress on LIE: bi-LYE. It rhymes with *rely*.
words.fact: From Old English *beleogan*, 'to deceive by lying': the prefix *be-* + *lie* (to tell an untruth). The appearance, as it were, tells a lie about the reality.
words.trap: *Belie* is not *believe* and not *betray* in the sense of 'reveal'. *Her smile belied her fear* = the smile hid it; *her shaking hands betrayed her fear* = they revealed it.
distractor_traps: Recall reports do not give the options. The predictable traps are verbs that keep appearance and reality in line: *reflect*, *reveal*, *attest to*, *underscore*. Look for a contrast signal (*although*, *yet*, *despite*) near the blank.
Work out which side is the subject. If the subject is the surface (a title, a tone, a plain exterior), expect sense (1); if it is the evidence, expect sense (2).
words.tip: be·[lie]: the surface tells a *lie* about what is underneath.

words.def: To buttress an argument, a claim or a system is to give it support and make it stronger.
words.sat_sense: Figurative verb: strengthen or defend a claim with evidence (College Board's gloss is 'strengthen, defend'). The literal noun is a stone support built against a wall.
ex: The author buttresses her argument with wage data from three separate industries.
Fah buttressed her case for a later library closing time with a survey of two hundred classmates.
words.grammar: Transitive: *buttress + claim / argument / position (+ with evidence)*; passive *be buttressed by*. Regular: *buttresses, buttressed, buttressing*.
words.say: /ˈbʌtrəs/: two syllables, BUT-ruhs. The second vowel is weak; it does not rhyme with *dress*.
words.fact: From Old French *bouterez*, probably from *bouter*, 'to push against'. Medieval builders pushed stone buttresses against high walls to keep them from falling outwards; writers have used the word of arguments for almost as long.
words.trap: You buttress something that already stands: a claim, a wall, a position. You do not buttress a person, and it is not *butter* or *button*.

Its opposite, *undermine*, is the same building metaphor in reverse (digging under a wall). If the passage's evidence weakens the claim, *buttress* is the trap.
words.tip: Picture a stone prop pushing against a tall stone wall: evidence pushes the same way against a wobbling claim.

words.def: To mitigate something harmful is to make it less serious, less severe or less painful.
words.sat_sense: Lessen the force of a harm or risk without removing it. Midway on the remedy-to-worsen scale: the harm is still there, only smaller.
ex: Wetlands mitigate the impact of floods by absorbing water that would otherwise rush downstream.
Starting the sports day at seven mitigated the worst of the heat, although by ten the track was still too hot to touch.
family: unmitigated (adj: complete, usually of something bad)
words.grammar: Transitive: *mitigate + risk / damage / effects / impact*. The object is the harm itself. The verb takes no preposition: not *mitigate against*.
words.say: /ˈmɪtɪɡeɪt/: three syllables, stress on MIT: MIT-i-gayt.
words.fact: From Latin *mitigare*, 'to soften': *mitis* ('mild, gentle') + *agere* ('to do, to make'). Literally, to make mild. *Unmitigated* keeps the idea: an unmitigated disaster is one that nothing softened.
words.trap: *Militate against* (work against) is a different verb; *mitigate against* is a well-known mistake. Mitigate does not mean prevent or solve.
distractor_traps: Official Hard item options: *presuppose*, *categorize*, *validate*. These are thinking verbs; the blank needed something done to a harm. *Validate* tempts because it is positive, but you validate a claim, not a flood.

Strength check within the field: *mitigate* (less severe) is weaker than *ameliorate* (actually better), and both are weaker than *rectify* or *eliminate*. A passage saying the problem 'remains' wants the weaker verb.
words.tip: [mit]·igate: make it *mild* (Latin *mitis*). The damage is still there, but milder.

words.def: To stymie a person, a plan or an effort is to block it so that it cannot make progress.
words.sat_sense: Block or thwart (College Board's gloss is 'prevent, greatly hinder'). The 'block' corner of the remedy/worsen/cause/block field, stronger than *hinder* or *impede*.

patterns.title: Every claim stands on a ladder of strength
patterns.insight: SAT passages are about research, and research is about how far a claim can be trusted. Six of the thirty items mark rungs on one ladder. At the bottom a claim is *untenable* (it cannot be defended at all); one rung up it is *tenuous* (it stands, but on thin support). A claim rises when someone *substantiates* it (supplies evidence for it, possibly their own), when finds or records *attest to* it (the evidence itself bears witness), when the writer *buttresses* it (adds further props), and highest of all when an independent second source *corroborates* it. One verb pulls the other way: evidence that *belies* a claim shows the claim to be false. The test almost never asks 'is the claim supported?'; it asks 'how strongly, and by whom?', so the wrong options are usually words from another rung.
examples: One unsigned postcard: the claim is *tenuous*. No evidence that survives questioning: it is *untenable*.
The author adds wage data to *buttress* her own argument; a rival team's separate experiment *corroborates* it.
Shell beads found far inland *attest to* long-distance trade; a finding that the beads were made locally would *belie* it.
patterns.drill: Put these in order from weakest to strongest support for a claim, saying each aloud: corroborated, tenuous, substantiated, untenable. Then name the verb from this card that knocks a claim down.

patterns.title: One line for problems: start it, worsen it, soften it, improve it
patterns.insight: Five verbs describe what happens to a problem, and they differ only in direction and distance. To *precipitate* a problem is to set it off suddenly. To *exacerbate* it is to make an existing problem worse. To *mitigate* it is to make its harm less severe while the problem remains. To *ameliorate* it is to make the situation actually better. Beyond that lies *rectify* (put it right). *Stymie* belongs to a different sentence: its object is not the problem but someone's effort or progress, which it blocks. So two questions settle most items in this field. First, the direction: is the passage making things better or worse? Second, the object: is the blank acting on a harm, a situation, or an attempt? The back-test is a warning about this very set: 'remedy' words were keys in three earlier official tests and in none of the next three, so learn the line, not a favourite word.
examples: The drought *precipitated* a food shortage; hoarding *exacerbated* it; imports *mitigated* its effects; a good harvest *ameliorated* the situation.
Relief efforts were *stymied* by flooded roads (the efforts are blocked, not the flood).
'Did not solve the problem, but...' signals *mitigate* or *ameliorate*; 'instead' after a hoped-for cure signals *exacerbate*.
patterns.drill: Draw a line with a minus sign at the left and a plus sign at the right. Place exacerbate, mitigate, ameliorate and rectify on it in ten seconds, then say what kind of object *stymie* and *precipitate* each need.

patterns.title: Hidden or showing: latent and manifest, opaque and clear
patterns.insight: Four items answer the question 'can you see it?'. *Latent* and *manifest* are a true opposite pair about the thing itself: a latent quality is present but not yet showing; when it shows, it has become manifest. *Opaque* is about the viewer's side: the thing may be fully there, but you cannot see into it or understand how it works; its opposite is *transparent* or *clear*. *Belie* handles the case where what shows is misleading: the surface tells a different story from the reality. Its mirror image is *attest to*, where the surface is honest evidence of what lies beneath. This field is almost absent from Easy official items and common in Hard ones, so it matters most to students who reach the harder second module.
examples: Her talent was *latent* until the audition; by the final scene it was *manifest* in every gesture.
The rules are not hidden, just *opaque*: everyone can read them, and no one can follow them.
A calm voice *belied* her nerves (surface and truth differ); her shaking hands *attested to* them (surface and truth agree).
patterns.drill: For each sentence, say latent, manifest, opaque or belies: (1) the anger showed in every line of the letter; (2) the anger was there but had not yet surfaced; (3) nobody could work out what the letter meant; (4) the polite greeting gave no hint of the anger that followed.

patterns.title: How much does it matter? From the centre to the edge and off the map
patterns.insight: Picture a target. At the centre is whatever is *integral to* the whole: remove it and the whole fails. Further out is what is *peripheral to* it: connected, but at the edge. Off the target altogether is what is *inconsequential to* it (nothing follows from it) or *immaterial to* it (it does not bear on the question). The last two are near-synonyms with a different angle: *inconsequential* judges effects, *immaterial* judges relevance to a decision or argument. All four take *to*. SAT passages use this scale when a scholar re-ranks something: what was thought minor turns out to be essential, or the reverse, and a contrast word (*instead*, *far from*, *merely*) tells you which way the passage is moving. *A dearth of* is a neighbour from the quantity scale: it says how much of something exists, not how much it matters.
examples: Once seen as *peripheral to* the story, the servant's letters are now thought *integral to* it.
The paint colour is *immaterial to* the judges' decision; a two-baht price rise is *inconsequential to* most buyers.
'Far from being ___, the chorus...' wants an edge word in the blank, because *far from* will overturn it.
patterns.drill: Say whether each is integral, peripheral or immaterial to winning a 100-metre race: the runner's start; the colour of her shoelaces; the warm-up music. Then put each answer in a full sentence with *to*.

patterns.title: Alike, unlike, out of place, out of pattern
patterns.insight: Four items describe fit, and each needs a different number of things. *Homogeneous* and *disparate* both describe a whole set: its members are all of one kind, or of kinds so different they resist comparison. *An anomaly* is one case set against a pattern: thirty-nine results agree and the fortieth does not. *Incongruous with* is one thing set against its surroundings or against what is expected: a steel door on a brick cottage. So before choosing, count: is the passage talking about a set, about one case and a pattern, or about one thing and its setting? Two Greek roots hold the field together: *homos*, 'same', is in *homogeneous* and, less visibly, in *anomaly* (*an-* + *homalos*, 'not even'); *genos*, 'kind', is the second half of *homogeneous* and of its opposite, *heterogeneous*.
examples: A *homogeneous* sample: two hundred first-year students from one university. A *disparate* one: sailors, farmers and schoolchildren.
One falling tide gauge among thirty-nine rising ones is an *anomaly*.
The cheerful ending is *incongruous with* the bleak chapters before it.
patterns.drill: Look round the classroom and name, in a sentence each: one homogeneous set, one disparate set, one thing that is incongruous with the room, and one anomaly in a pattern you can see.

patterns.title: A dozen Latin and Greek roots carry most of the list
patterns.insight: Most of the thirty are Latin or Greek compounds, and their roots recur across the SAT's vocabulary. *Tangere*, 'to touch', gives *contingent* (touching, so dependent), *integral* (untouched, so whole) and the official distractor *tangential* (touching only at the edge). *Valere*, 'to be strong', gives *prevail* (be stronger) and *ambivalent* (strong both ways), with *valid* and *prevalent*. *Testis*, 'witness', gives *attest*, *testify* and *testimony*. *Robur*, 'oak', gives *corroborate* and *robust*. *Melior*, 'better', gives *ameliorate*; *acer*, 'sharp', gives *exacerbate*, *acid* and *acerbic*; *mitis*, 'mild', gives *mitigate*. *Sequi*, 'to follow', gives *inconsequential*, *sequence* and *consequently*. *Stare*, 'to stand', gives *substantiate* (stand under). *Caput*, 'head', gives *precipitate* (head first). Greek *homos*, 'same', gives *homogeneous* and *anomaly*; *peri*, 'around', gives *peripheral*. Among the content words, three have no classical root to lean on: *belie* and *dearth* are native English (be- + lie; dear + -th), and *stymie* is a golf word of uncertain origin. Roots are a memory aid, not a decoding trick: *sanguine* is from 'blood', and no amount of Latin will tell you it means hopeful.
examples: *tangere* (touch), root in brackets: con·[ting]·ent, in·[teg]·ral, [tang]·ential, [tang]·ible. (Brackets mark the root, not the stress.)
*valere* (be strong): pre·[vail], ambi·[val]·ent, [val]·id, pre·[val]·ent.
*robur* (oak): cor·[rob]·orate and [rob]·ust; *acer* (sharp): ex·[acer]·bate and [ac]·id.
patterns.drill: Cover the list. From each root, name one of the thirty and one everyday relative: tangere, valere, testis, robur, melior, acer, sequi. Seven roots in sixty seconds.

patterns.title: Word-building: the 'not' prefixes and the -ate verbs
patterns.insight: Two building rules cover half the list. First, the 'not' family. Latin *in-* means 'not' and changes shape before certain letters: *in-consequential*, *in-congruous*, but *im-material* before m. Greek *a-/an-* does the same job in *an-omaly*, and English *un-* in *untenable*. Strip the prefix and you usually find a positive word worth knowing: *consequential*, *congruent*, *material* (= relevant), *tenable*. Two warnings. *Integral* hides a 'not' you no longer feel (in- + touch = untouched, whole), so it is positive. And *dis-* in *disparate* means 'apart', not 'not'. Second, the *-ate* verbs: *corroborate, ameliorate, mitigate, exacerbate, substantiate, precipitate*. They descend from Latin past participles in *-atus*, and they behave alike. As verbs the ending is a full /eɪt/ ('ayt'), and the main stress falls two syllables before it: kuh-ROB-uh-rayt, MIT-i-gayt, ig-ZAS-uh-bayt, suhb-STAN-shee-ayt, pri-SIP-i-tayt. *Ameliorate* is the exception: it has five syllables, /əˈmiː.li.ə.reɪt/, with the stress three syllables before the ending: uh-MEE-lee-uh-rayt. The noun adds *-ion* and moves the main stress onto the A: kuh-rob-uh-RAY-shuhn, mit-i-GAY-shuhn. When an *-ate* word is an adjective, the ending weakens to /ət/: *disparate* is DIS-puh-ruht, and the adjective *precipitate* (hasty) ends the same way.
examples: [in]·consequential; [in]·congruous; [im]·material; [an]·omaly (an- + homalos). Positive partners: consequential, congruent, material.
Verb /eɪt/: they *corroborate* (kuh-ROB-uh-rayt). Noun: *corroboration* (kuh-rob-uh-RAY-shuhn).
Adjective /ət/: *disparate* sources (DIS-puh-ruht); a *precipitate* decision (pri-SIP-i-tuht).
patterns.drill: Read aloud as verb, then as -ation noun, tapping the stressed syllable: mitigate, exacerbate, corroborate, substantiate, precipitate, ameliorate. Then give the positive partner of immaterial, inconsequential and incongruous.

patterns.title: The preposition is half the answer
patterns.insight: The digital SAT does not test idioms in the everyday sense (no 'raining cats and dogs'). What looks idiom-like is the dependent preposition: a word that always brings the same small word with it. Between 16% and 21% of official vocabulary keys are multi-word, at every difficulty. The prepositions are not random; each carries a picture. *On* is resting on: *contingent on*, like *depend on* and *rely on*. *To* points at the thing a judgement is made against: *integral to, peripheral to, inconsequential to, immaterial to*, and evidence that *attests to* a fact. *With* sets two things side by side to see whether they match: *incongruous with*, like *consistent with*. *Over* is on top, the winner: *prevail over*. *For* is in place of: *a proxy for*, like *a substitute for*. *Of* measures a quantity: *a dearth of*. *In* marks where something shows: *manifest in*. *About* or *toward(s)* aims a feeling: *ambivalent about*, *sanguine about*. One caution from the official items: all four options normally come with their own correct preposition (*controversial among, antagonistic toward, imitated by*), so grammar alone will not eliminate them. Learn the phrase as one unit of meaning.
examples: Survival is *contingent on* rain. Pit size is *a proxy for* wealth. The colour is *immaterial to* the result.
The steel door is *incongruous with* the brick walls. The safer design *prevailed over* its rival.
The beads *attest to* trade; her debt to tradition is *manifest in* the courtyards; critics were *ambivalent about* the ending.
patterns.drill: Cover the right-hand words and supply the preposition in under a minute: contingent ___, a proxy ___, immaterial ___, incongruous ___, attest ___, prevail ___, a dearth ___, manifest ___, integral ___, ambivalent ___.

patterns.title: Concrete first, abstract on the test
patterns.insight: Many of the thirty began as words for physical things, and the SAT uses the abstract sense that grew out of them. A *buttress* is a stone prop against a wall; evidence buttresses a claim. *Opaque* glass blocks light; opaque prose blocks understanding. *Peripheral* vision is at the edge of sight; a peripheral issue is at the edge of the argument. *Tenuous* meant thin; a tenuous link is a thin thread. To *precipitate* was to throw down head first, and chemists and weather forecasters still use it for things that fall; a crisis is precipitated when it comes down all at once. *Immaterial* meant not made of matter, and now means not mattering. *Sanguine* meant full of blood, and so rosy and hopeful. A *proxy* was a person acting for another, and is now a measurement acting for another. The dictionary often labels only the concrete sense (Oxford marks the noun *buttress*, the noun *peripheral* and the chemistry noun *precipitate*, and leaves the SAT sense without a level), which is why so many of these cards read 'unlabelled'. The official 'most nearly means' items are built on the same idea in reverse: an everyday word used in a less common sense, as when *manifest* meant 'perceptible'.
examples: Stone *buttress* on a wall, then data *buttressing* a theory.
*Opaque* bathroom glass, then an *opaque* tax rule.
A ship's *manifest* lists what is on board; a *manifest* error is one anybody can see.
patterns.drill: Choose three of buttress, opaque, peripheral, tenuous, precipitate. For each, say one sentence with the physical meaning and one with the abstract meaning.

patterns.title: How the three wrong answers are built
patterns.insight: Official wrong options are not random hard words; they come in recognisable kinds. (1) Same field, opposite direction: *exacerbating* beside the key *redressing*; *profusion of* beside *paucity of*; *operative* beside *latent*. (2) Same field, different relationship: *unobtrusive* and *concealed* (about visibility) beside *peripheral* (about importance); *compound* (worsen a difficulty) beside *stymie* (block an effort). (3) Same register, different job: *circumvent, disseminate, implement* beside *corroborate* are all things researchers do, but not to a claim. (4) Same grammar frame: every option is adjective + preposition, so only meaning separates *inconsequential to* from *antagonistic toward*. Sound-alikes (*collaborate* for *corroborate*, *desperate* for *disparate*, *ambiguous* for *ambivalent*) rarely appear as printed options; they are mistakes students bring with them. Three facts from the official data keep expectations honest. At Hard level the distractors are as rare as the keys. The key is the rarest of the four options in about 31% of Hard items and the plainest in about 16%, so 'pick the hardest word' and 'avoid the hardest word' both fail. And about 13% of Question Bank keys also serve as a wrong option in another item, which is why *ambivalent*, *substantiate*, *exacerbate* and *incongruous* are on this list although they are mostly evidenced as distractors.
examples: Blank needs 'make better'; the options include *exacerbate*. Kind 1: right field, wrong direction.
Blank needs 'not central'; the options include *concealed*. Kind 2: nearby field, wrong relationship.
Blank needs 'support with evidence'; the options include *implement*. Kind 3: right register, wrong job.
patterns.drill: Take any mini-item on the cards. Before looking at the key, label each wrong option 1, 2, 3 or 4 by the kinds above. One item, one minute.

fields.name: Strength of a claim
fields.description: How well a claim is supported, and what evidence does to it: from weak (*tenuous*) to supported twice over (*corroborate*). The largest Question Bank field (evidence, claims and reasoning: 44 of 261 keys).

fields.name: Remedy, worsen, cause, block
fields.description: What an action does to a problem or an effort: start it (*precipitate*), worsen it (*exacerbate*), soften it (*mitigate*), improve it (*ameliorate*), or stop an effort dead (*stymie*). Question Bank field 'helping, hindering and causing': 33 of 261 keys.

fields.name: Hidden, visible, clarity
fields.description: Whether something shows (*manifest*), lies hidden (*latent*), cannot be seen into (*opaque*), or shows a false face (*belie*). Almost absent from Easy items; 9 of 61 Hard keys.

fields.name: Centre, edge, relevance (and extent)
fields.description: How much something matters to the whole: essential (*integral to*), marginal (*peripheral to*), or of no effect (*inconsequential to*, *immaterial to*). The extent phrase *a dearth of* is filed here, as the first report's 'widespread or marginal' set was.

fields.name: Fit, mismatch, anomaly
fields.description: Whether things are alike (*homogeneous*), unlike (*disparate*), out of place (*incongruous with*) or out of pattern (*anomaly*). Part of the Question Bank's similarity-and-difference field (38 of 261 keys).

fields.name: Attitude and temperament
fields.description: A person's stance or outlook: hopeful (*sanguine*) or pulled two ways (*ambivalent*). Question Bank field 'attitude, stance and disposition': 17 of 261 keys.

fields.name: Dependence and relationship
fields.description: How two things are tied: one is a condition of the other (*contingent on*), stands in for it (*a proxy for*) or defeats it (*prevail over*). The first report under-weighted this field; the Question Bank does not.

fields.name: Transitions (outside the seven fields)
fields.description: Logical links tested in Transitions questions, not Words in Context: concession (*that said*) and fitting result (*accordingly*). Included because both carry a C1 level (*accordingly*: Oxford visible badge; *that said*: Oxford page markup, not displayed) and three official keys each.
